title: Section check: Culture, Society & Identity
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 15–19. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: A player sees a football shirt as part of the team. A fan sees it as a happy memory. They have different perspectives. What does perspective mean?

options.text: A person who makes things with their hands or tools
options.feedback: Not quite. That is a maker. The player and the fan did not make the shirt. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: The way one person sees or thinks about something
options.feedback: Yes. A perspective is the way one person sees something. The player and the fan see the same shirt in different ways.

options.text: A picture or shape that stands for an idea
options.feedback: Not quite. That is a symbol. Here, each person sees the shirt in their own way. Look back at Lesson 15.

stimulus.title: A made-up drum: three notes
items: The seller says it is for playing music at events.
The owner says it reminds her of the day she joined a music club.
The maker says an older drummer taught her the pattern.

questions.question: A museum wants a label for this drum. Which label is best, based on Lesson 15?

options.text: The pattern is a symbol of the whole town and all its people.
options.feedback: Not quite. No note says what the pattern means. A good label does not guess. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: It is just an everyday drum. It has no other meaning for anyone.
options.feedback: Not quite. The notes show that the drum also holds a memory and a skill. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: For music. It holds a memory for its owner and a skill for its maker.
options.feedback: Yes. This label uses what the seller, the owner and the maker say. It does not guess what the pattern means.

questions.question: At Hillside Learning Centre, a volunteer talks about the food notice. Some visitors read the notice in English. Others use the pictures, sign language or help from a friend. What does this show?

options.text: People can understand one message in different ways.
options.feedback: Yes. Visitors use words, pictures, sign language or a friend's help. They all get the same message in different ways.

options.text: Most visitors do not want to read the notice.
options.feedback: Not quite. The visitors do want the message. They use different ways to understand it. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: Only people who read English can come to the centre.
options.feedback: Not quite. The notice says the food is for everyone. Many visitors understand it without reading English. Look back at Lesson 16.

questions.question: Lesson 16 says that no language is better than another. What reason does it give?

options.text: All languages use the very same words for things.
options.feedback: Not quite. Languages have different words, and they borrow words from each other. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: Each language is spoken by the same number of people.
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson does not count speakers. It talks about what each language holds. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: Each one holds the stories of its speakers.
options.feedback: Yes. Every language holds the knowledge and stories of its speakers. So no language is the best.

questions.question: In a made-up village, older weavers show young people how to make baskets. Later, the young people will teach others. Which word from Lesson 17 names this?

options.text: A celebration
options.feedback: Not quite. A celebration marks a special day with others. Here, older people pass a skill to younger people. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Transmission
options.feedback: Yes. Transmission means passing knowledge or skills from one person to another. The weavers pass on their skill.

options.text: A purpose
options.feedback: Not quite. A purpose is the reason why something is done. Here, older people pass a skill to younger people. Look back at Lesson 17.

questions.question: What does Lesson 17 say about traditions that change?

options.text: A tradition can change and still keep its purpose.
options.feedback: Yes. The community meal starts earlier and adds new dishes. It still helps people meet, teach and welcome others.

options.text: A tradition ends as soon as people change it.
options.feedback: Not quite. People adapt traditions to fit new times, and the meal still goes on. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Only the very oldest way of doing it is the right way.
options.feedback: Not quite. Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt them to fit new times. Look back at Lesson 17.

questions.question: Lesson 18 gives three examples: rock art in Algeria, a painted scroll in China and sand drawings in Vanuatu. What do they all show?

options.text: Art from long ago is always about animals.
options.feedback: Not quite. The rock art shows animals, but the scroll shows a busy city full of people. Look back at Lesson 18.

options.text: People around the world tell stories with art.
options.feedback: Yes. The three examples come from different parts of the world. In each place, people use art to tell stories and keep knowledge.

options.text: Only one part of the world tells stories with art.
options.feedback: Not quite. The three examples come from three different places. People all over the world tell stories with art. Look back at Lesson 18.

stimulus.title: A made-up mural
stimulus.body: A mural is a big painting on a wall. This one is on the wall of a made-up school. It shows a tall tree with long roots. Children of different heights hold hands around the tree. At the top are the words “We grow together”.

questions.question: Which sentence is an interpretation of the mural?

options.text: The mural may be about working as a team.
options.feedback: Yes. This is an idea about what the mural means. The joined hands and the words support it, and “may” shows you are careful.

options.text: Children hold hands around a tall tree.
options.feedback: Not quite. This is an observation. Anyone can check it by looking at the mural. Look back at Lesson 18.

options.text: The words at the top say “We grow together”.
options.feedback: Not quite. This is an observation. Anyone can read the words on the wall. Look back at Lesson 18.

questions.question: A made-up art club writes its meeting times in only one language. Some members cannot read that language, so they miss meetings. Which word from Lesson 19 names this problem?

options.text: Agency
options.feedback: Not quite. Agency is the power to make choices and act. This problem makes it hard to take part. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: An opinion
options.feedback: Not quite. An opinion is what a person thinks about something. This problem makes it hard to take part. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: A barrier
options.feedback: Yes. A barrier makes it harder for someone to take part. The club could share its times in more than one way.

questions.question: What does Lesson 19 say a group can do so that more people feel they belong?

options.text: Ask new members to share private things
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says nobody should have to share private things to belong. Look back at Lesson 19.

options.text: Change the way the group works
options.feedback: Yes. The club does not need to change its members. It can change how it works, for example with turn-taking rules.

options.text: Ask members to act like everyone else
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says a group should change how it works, not change its members. Look back at Lesson 19.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how people share meaning and help others belong.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 15–19, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
